common_name: Royal Crown Turnip (Purple-Topped Dual-Purpose Hybrid Turnip)

planting.note: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, and again in late summer for a fall crop; roots mature quickly and hold quality well at either end of the cool season.

directions: Royal Crown is a fast-maturing F1 hybrid turnip grown for both its roots and its abundant dark green tops, making it a genuine dual-purpose crop rather than a greens-only or roots-only type. The slightly flattened, globe-shaped roots are smooth and creamy white with a bright purple-blotched crown, and stay sweet and mild if pulled small rather than left to size up. Because the leafy top is unusually productive relative to the root, it is a good choice for gardeners who want a steady cutting of turnip greens alongside a modest root harvest. Direct sow shallowly into loose soil and thin early, since crowded roots become misshapen.

common_name: Manchester Market Turnip (English Heirloom Green-Top Turnip)

planting.note: Direct sow for a fall crop in late summer; this variety tolerates a later sowing date than many turnips, so it is also useful as a follow-on crop after an early planting has been harvested.

directions: Manchester Market is a 19th-century English field and market turnip named for the city where it was widely grown for sale, producing a creamy white, globe-shaped root topped with light green, edible foliage. It carries a stronger, more peppery bite than modern salad turnips once roots size up past tennis-ball diameter, which suits it well to stews and long-cooked dishes rather than raw eating. It is notably forgiving of a later sowing date than many turnip varieties, making it a practical choice for filling a gap after an earlier crop is cleared. Harvest at a moderate size for the best balance of texture and flavor, since older roots turn fibrous.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, since germination is slow, and transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing; Ibis tolerates an early, cool start better than many celeriac types.

directions: Ibis is a fast-developing celeriac prized by market growers for its smooth, oval-round white globes that clean up with minimal peeling loss compared to older, knobbier types. Its strong field resistance to septoria leaf spot keeps the canopy healthy through the long season needed to size up a root, and its bolt-hardiness makes it a reasonable choice for an early start under cover. As with all celeriac, keep the bed evenly and continuously moist, since inconsistent watering cracks and hollows the developing globe, and strip away side shoots through summer to concentrate growth into the root. Harvest in fall for a dense, long-storing root with a clean, nutty celery flavor.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since germination is slow and seedling growth is sluggish at first; transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing.

directions: Alabaster is a light-skinned celeriac whose pale flesh discolors noticeably less than many other varieties once peeled or cooked, an advantage for cooks who want a bright white puree or gratin. The globes are typically smaller and more rounded than some maincrop celeriac, with a strong, clean celery flavor and good storage life in a root cellar. Grow exactly as other celeriac: start early indoors given the slow germination, transplant into deep, fertile, constantly moist soil, and remove developing side roots through the season to channel growth into a single dense globe. Harvest in fall after light frost, which improves the flavor.

planting.note: Direct sow in loose, deeply worked, stone-free soil; scorzonera is a long-season root that benefits from a full cool season and can be left in the ground through winter and dug as needed.

directions: Duplex is a long-cultivated Continental European scorzonera selected for heavy, uniform yields of long, black-skinned, white-fleshed roots and for notable resistance to bolting compared with older strains. Direct sow into deeply loosened soil, since the taproot resents disturbance and will fork in compacted or stony ground, and thin seedlings early to give roots room to size up straight. The cooked root has a sweet, mild, faintly oyster-like flavor similar to salsify, and is traditionally peeled, cut into pieces, and steamed or simmered before finishing with a sauce. Roots can be left in the ground over winter in most climates and lifted through the cold months, with flavor improving after frost.

common_name: Green Boy Komatsuna (Cold-Tolerant Hybrid Japanese Mustard Spinach)

planting.note: Direct sow from early spring into fall; Green Boy holds up to cold better than most komatsuna, so it is a good choice for late-fall and even overwintered plantings in mild climates.

directions: Green Boy is a modern komatsuna hybrid selected for compact, glossy, deep green leaves on pale, tender petioles, with a flavor that sits between spinach and mild mustard. It stands out among komatsuna types for its cold tolerance, continuing to produce usable leaves well into cool weather when other Asian greens have stalled or bolted, which extends the harvest window in fall and early winter. Direct sow and harvest young for salad-size baby leaves or let plants develop further for bunching greens suited to stir-fries and quick braises. Succession sow every few weeks in the cooler shoulder seasons for a steady supply.

planting.note: Direct sow from early spring through fall; Misome tolerates heat better than tatsoi and can be sown in successive batches through the warmer months for a continuous supply.

directions: Misome is a relatively recent Japanese cross between komatsuna and tatsoi, combining tatsoi's glossy, savoyed, rounded leaf with a more upright, komatsuna-like growth habit that is easier to harvest cleanly. The thick, tender leaves and stems have a sweet, mild flavor raw that turns more robust and mustardy once cooked, and the plant holds up well in the field without turning tough or bitter. It matures quickly from direct sowing and shows good tolerance of both heat and cool weather, making it a flexible filler green for spring, summer, and fall plantings. Harvest whole heads or take outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again crop.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed as soon as soil is workable in spring, in deep, loose, stone-free ground; parsnip seed loses viability quickly, so use current-year seed.

directions: Panache is a vigorous modern F1 parsnip that produces long, wedge-shaped roots with notably smooth white skin and sweet, creamy flesh, developed as a rival to show-quality types while remaining practical for ordinary garden use. It combines good field resistance to canker with strong storage quality, holding well in the ground or in cool storage after harvest. Sow shallowly into loosened, stone-free soil and keep the seedbed consistently moist, since parsnip germinates slowly and unevenly and dry spells reduce stands further. As with all parsnips, delay harvest until after one or more hard frosts, which convert root starches to sugars for noticeably sweeter roots.
